title: XRP Large Wallets Keep Growing Through a 30% Slide Toward $1.05
summary: XRP wallets holding at least 10,000 tokens increased as the cryptocurrency fell roughly 30% over seven weeks, according to Santiment. The firm viewed the divergence as an accumulation signal, with $1 emerging as the immediate price level to defend. XRP Large Wallet Count Expands During Price Decline...
content:
XRP wallets holding at least 10,000 tokens increased as the cryptocurrency fell roughly 30% over seven weeks, according to Santiment. The firm viewed the divergence as an accumulation signal, with $1 emerging as the immediate price level to defend.

Key Takeaways

  • About 343,500 XRP wallets held at least 10,000 tokens.
  • The category gained 16,815 addresses, or 5.15%, over nine months.
  • Losing $1 as wallet growth reverses could bring a short-term sell-off.

XRP Large Wallet Count Expands During Price Decline

Blockchain analytics firm Santiment highlighted growth in large XRP wallets on Nov. 11 as the cryptocurrency fell roughly 30% over seven weeks. In its XRP large-wallet assessment, shared on X, the firm stated:

“XRP wallets holding at least 10K tokens are growing at a rapid rate here in November. There are now roughly 343.5K of these wallets, up 16,815 (+5.15%) in 9 months. Larger holders are expanding even as XRP falls toward $1.05.”

The firm interpreted this divergence, or opposing movement in price and wallet counts, as accumulation, meaning some holders were adding XRP to their positions. Santiment noted: “When larger holders keep appearing during a selloff, it suggests some higher-capital traders are using the fear to build positions instead of abandoning XRP.”

Wallet Counts Reflect Balances and Custody Arrangements

A separate measure had already shown growth among wallets with substantially larger balances. Santiment counted 2,147 wallets holding at least 1 million XRP on Nov. 3, the category’s highest tally of the year. That group had gained 28 addresses over 10 days, covering a different balance threshold and measurement period.

Santiment’s holder-distribution methodology groups addresses by token balance and distinguishes their number from their combined holdings. Crossing the 10,000-XRP threshold increases the qualifying count; dropping below it reduces the tally. The increase therefore establishes growth in that category, while purchase volume requires separate evidence.

Ownership also differs from the number of addresses recorded on the ledger. Exchanges and other providers can use shared XRP Ledger addresses, identifying customers through destination tags, numeric codes attached to payments. A single qualifying address can consequently represent funds belonging to multiple people.

Changes in custody can also affect where balances appear. Moving assets into self-custody of crypto holdings places them in wallets whose private keys the holder controls. Such a transfer can change the distribution of balances without representing a new purchase.

Santiment Ties XRP’s Next Move to $1 and Large-Wallet Growth

Santiment remarked:

“$1.00 is now the key XRP level to defend.”

XRP traded at $1.06 at 5:17 p.m. EST on Nov. 11, above the $1 level Santiment flagged, after swinging between $1.05 and $1.08 over the previous 24 hours. The token stood 18.61% below its $1.31 price a week earlier, 22.35% below $1.37 a month earlier, and 55.93% below $2.41 a year earlier.

For its Nov. 11 outlook, the firm tied a potential recovery toward $1.10-$1.15 to XRP holding $1, continued growth in wallets holding at least 10,000 tokens, and bitcoin stabilizing. A loss of $1 alongside a reversal in wallet growth would likely trigger a short-term sell-off, the firm assessed. It also anticipated that retail fear following such a decline could quickly lead to a bounce.

Broader address creation had strengthened earlier in November. Santiment reported 7,934 new XRP wallets on Nov. 1, the sixth-highest daily total of the year. That activity measured new addresses, a separate indicator from growth among wallets above a holding threshold.

Trading positions provided a contrasting signal. Among the most profitable XRP wallets tracked by Santiment, three active short sellers added about 2.1 million XRP to their positions since late October, the firm said Nov. 6. That directional trading exposure reflected bets on falling prices; spot-wallet balances measure XRP held directly in wallets.

title: Bitcoin Faces Deeper Reset Risk as Bitfinex Warns of $70K Drop
summary: Bitfinex warned that bitcoin risked a prolonged decline as weak fund flows, uneven corporate demand, and broader market pressures tested its recovery. The exchange also flagged growing futures exposure and steeper altcoin losses. Bitcoin Faces a $75,717 Recovery Test Crypto exchange Bitfinex warned ...
content:
Bitfinex warned that bitcoin risked a prolonged decline as weak fund flows, uneven corporate demand, and broader market pressures tested its recovery. The exchange also flagged growing futures exposure and steeper altcoin losses.

Key Takeaways

  • Bitcoin spent four days below its $75,717 recovery threshold.
  • Futures exposure increased 3.3% while prices declined 2.6%.
  • Bitfinex outlined a conditional decline toward $70,000-$71,200.

Bitcoin Faces a $75,717 Recovery Test

Crypto exchange Bitfinex warned Nov. 11 that bitcoin risked a deeper reset, meaning a prolonged decline, after four days below its $75,717 short-term holder cost basis. That level represented the estimated average acquisition price of coins held for fewer than 155 days. Regaining it was central to the exchange’s recovery assessment.

Among 14 comparable episodes since 2016, bitcoin regained the threshold within two weeks in 11 cases; three took 57 to 114 days. The current break began Nov. 8, making Nov. 22 the two-week checkpoint. Bitfinex stated:

“Rallies towards the short-term holder cost basis at $75,717 are likely to be sold until spot demand returns.”

Prices rebounded above $74,600 around 12:25 p.m. EST on Nov. 11, remaining below that threshold. Bitcoin eased to $74,157 by 5:35 p.m. EST, up 0.68% over 24 hours but down 7.15% over the week, 10.42% over the month, and 27.68% over the year.

Futures Positions Rise as Buyers Realize Losses

Aggregate futures open interest, the total exposure in contracts still open and unsettled, reached 701,900 BTC around the Nov. 11 daily open. Exposure rose 3.3% from Nov. 8 while prices declined 2.6%, reinforcing bitcoin derivatives pressure. Bitfinex warned that continued bullish positioning increased the risk of forced selling.

A measure dividing recent holders’ sale proceeds by acquisition costs reached 0.989 on Nov. 10, equivalent to receiving 98.9 cents per dollar spent. Separately, 1.6 million BTC bought between $75,000 and $80,000 was underwater, meaning worth less than its purchase price. Those holdings could create selling pressure during rebounds.

U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) lost approximately $399 million on Nov. 2. Corporate activity was mixed: Strategy Inc. (Nasdaq: MSTR) bought 1,036 BTC from Nov. 2-8, while MARA Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: MARA) disclosed selling 13,597 BTC over the past six weeks. Bitfinex concluded that corporate buying was insufficient to offset ETF selling.

Fund Flows and Broader Markets Shape the Outlook

Withdrawals subsequently slowed, with U.S. bitcoin ETF flows showing $201 million leaving Nov. 9 and $95 million Nov. 10. Bitfinex calculated $2.22 billion in net outflows across eight sessions beginning Oct. 30. Reclaiming $75,717 alongside three consecutive inflow sessions would support its correction scenario.

DWF Labs market insights lead Martin Lee offered a qualification to reliance on fund flows. He argued that fund withdrawals and deposits tended to follow price movements, limiting their predictive value.

Bitfinex also identified an imbalance in bitcoin’s relationship with equities. Across 25 sessions following the Nasdaq 100’s Oct. 6 record, bitcoin captured 91% of its losses on down days but 58% of its gains on up days. The index tracks 100 of the largest nonfinancial companies listed on Nasdaq.

Altcoin weakness extended the pressure beyond bitcoin. Across 12 large altcoins on Bitfinex, the median decline from the Sept. 21 close was 27.8%, compared with bitcoin’s 14.8%. Bitfinex attributed the gap to concentrated leverage and speculative capital moving elsewhere.

For the Nov. 13 options expiration, Bitfinex expected a $71,600-$75,800 range. A 10-year real Treasury yield, measured after accounting for expected inflation, above 2.8% or a Nasdaq 100 decline below 26,606 could trigger long liquidations. That conditional scenario pointed toward $70,000-$71,200.

title: BTC, ETH and XRP Fear Hits ‘Boiling Point’ as Rally Hopes Rise
summary: Santiment reported bearish social sentiment across bitcoin, ethereum, and XRP as cryptocurrency prices faced renewed pressure. The analytics firm argued that widespread pessimism could create conditions for a recovery, with XRP recording the weakest ratio among the three assets. Bearish Commentary O...
content:
Santiment reported bearish social sentiment across bitcoin, ethereum, and XRP as cryptocurrency prices faced renewed pressure. The analytics firm argued that widespread pessimism could create conditions for a recovery, with XRP recording the weakest ratio among the three assets.

Key Takeaways

  • XRP logged 49 bullish comments for every 100 bearish ones.
  • Bitcoin and ethereum also registered sentiment ratios below 1.0.
  • Bitcoin recovered above $74,000.

Bearish Commentary Outweighs Optimism Across Three Major Assets

Santiment, a crypto analytics firm that tracks online market discussion, shared its bitcoin, ethereum, and XRP sentiment readings on X on Nov. 10, opening with: “Retail fear is reaching a boiling point as crypto tests major lows!” It added:

“Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP sentiment has fallen deep into bearish territory according to our X, Reddit, Telegram and other social platform data.”

Bitcoin recorded 0.82 bullish comments per bearish one, compared with 0.88 for ethereum and 0.49 for XRP. The firm interpreted that pessimism as a potential contrarian signal, meaning one that runs against prevailing expectations. It explained: “Major cryptocurrency market rallies rarely begin when everyone expects one. They usually form while traders are fearful, selling losses, and doubting that prices can bounce at all.”

Bitcoin and Ether Edge Higher as Buying Demand Remains in Focus

As of this writing, bitcoin was trading at $74,032, up 0.42% over the preceding 24 hours. Ether traded at $2,056.62, gaining 0.33% over the same period. XRP changed hands at $1.05, a 0.33% decline.

Those moves followed bitcoin’s retreat below $74,000 on Nov. 10. Cryptocurrency market data provider Coinglass recorded approximately $356.16 million in crypto liquidations over the 24 hours ending around 8:45 a.m. Eastern time that day, with long positions absorbing $280.40 million.

Bitfinex analysts said a sustained recovery would depend in part on stronger demand from buyers purchasing bitcoin directly. Their Nov. 10 assessment also identified $75,900 to $77,500 as a potential selling zone, where renewed supply could pressure prices. The analysts expected bitcoin to trade within an options-implied range of $72,350 to $79,400 ahead of the Nov. 13 options expiry, with activity concentrated toward the lower end.

Ethereum Optimism Fades as XRP Fear Deepens

Social discussion feeds into Santiment’s social sentiment calculations, which sum positive and negative sentiment scores. The ratio compares bullish comments with bearish ones, so 0.82 represents about 82 positive remarks for every 100 negative ones. Parity is an equal balance at 1.0, with lower readings indicating more pessimism than optimism.

On Oct. 1, XRP logged a bullish-to-bearish ratio of 0.67, which Santiment described as its weakest sentiment since Aug. 17. The ether ratio was 0.89 in that update. XRP’s latest reading of 0.49 reflected a more negative balance than that earlier reading.

By Oct. 13, ethereum optimism contrasted with bitcoin and XRP fear. Ethereum’s ratio reached 2.05, with bitcoin at 0.82 and XRP at 0.92. Compared with those readings, bitcoin’s Nov. 10 ratio was unchanged, while ethereum turned negative and XRP’s balance deteriorated.

A relief rally is a temporary price rebound during a broader decline, while top caps are cryptocurrencies with the largest market values. Sentiment analysis evaluates investor emotions through social media, news, and other sources. Santiment projected:

“If we continue to see bearish commentary outweigh bullish commentary, especially for top caps, prices will inevitably see a strong relief rally.”

title: MSCI confirms Strategy’s removal from indexes at end of November
summary: Strategy, Metaplanet and Upexi are marked for deletion in MSCI’s final list, with changes taking effect after the Nov. 30 close.
content:
Index provider MSCI has confirmed Bitcoin treasury company Strategy will be removed from its global equity indexes, following months of debate over whether crypto treasury firms qualify as operating businesses.

MSCI’s final list of affected securities, released as part of its November index review, lists “STRATEGY A” with the action “Deleted.” Japan’s Metaplanet and crypto treasury company Upexi are also marked for deletion, while Ether treasury firm Sharplink is on a watchlist.

Strategy shares fell 1.65% in after-hours trading on Wednesday.

The changes take effect after market close on Nov. 30, under the implementation timetable MSCI announced in October.

Removal could prompt funds tracking the affected benchmarks to sell the companies’ shares, reducing a source of passive investment demand.

As Cointelegraph reported in October, JPMorgan previously estimated that Strategy’s exclusion could trigger roughly $2.8 billion in selling.

Strategy opposed the proposal, arguing that it repackaged MSCI’s earlier effort to exclude digital asset treasury companies and injected policy judgments into index construction.

The company nevertheless played down the potential disruption. In its consultation response, Strategy said MSCI-linked funds held approximately 13 million shares, representing 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding and less than one day’s trading volume.

Related: Bitcoin think tank questions MSCI’s ‘invisible committee’ over Strategy, Metaplanet rule

title: Strategy Loses MSCI Index Spot as Bitcoin Bet Faces New Test
summary: MSCI confirmed Strategy’s removal from its USA Index, setting up portfolio changes for funds tracking the benchmark. The decision followed a dispute over how the index provider classifies companies whose businesses center on holding assets. Funds Face Strategy’s November Index Exit Index provider MS...
content:
MSCI confirmed Strategy’s removal from its USA Index, setting up portfolio changes for funds tracking the benchmark. The decision followed a dispute over how the index provider classifies companies whose businesses center on holding assets.

Key Takeaways

  • Strategy joined 23 other stocks on the MSCI USA deletion list.
  • The company’s index exit takes effect after the Nov. 30 close.
  • Strategy previously put MSCI-linked holdings at 13 million shares.

Funds Face Strategy’s November Index Exit

Index provider MSCI named Strategy Inc. (Nasdaq: MSTR) for removal from its USA Index on Nov. 11. The benchmark tracks large and midsize U.S. companies. Its index review results identified “STRATEGY A,” the company’s publicly traded Class A common stock, which trades under the ticker MSTR.

Across the USA Index, the changes included 24 deletions, including Carlyle Group and Iren, with Moderna the sole addition. MSCI stated:

“Changes will be effective as of the close of business on November 30, 2026.”

The review used an Oct. 20 price cutoff and remained subject to adjustments for corporate events and other relevant developments before implementation.

Funds tracking the benchmark could sell Strategy shares as they adjust portfolios to reflect its removal. JPMorgan’s November 2025 estimate put potential MSCI-related selling at about $2.8 billion. The bank calculated that figure against an earlier digital asset exclusion proposal.

Eligibility Tests Replace Crypto-Specific Restrictions

The exclusion followed MSCI’s Oct. 15 decision to expand its non-operating company exclusions. That category covers investment funds and corporate issuers with similar financial characteristics.

Under the adopted eligibility framework, companies first undergo an assessment of whether they have substantial operating assets. Those failing face five financial tests covering assets, business expenses, cash flow, investment value changes, and reliance on outside funding. Four or more flags make a security ineligible, subject to buffers for existing constituents.

Existing members face removal only after failing the exclusion screen in each of their two most recent annual financial reports; MSCI may also consider interim reports covering shorter periods. With the November review, MSCI will end restrictions affecting firms whose digital assets represented at least half their total assets. Those freezes limited increases in shares counted for index calculations and proportions treated as available to foreign or domestic investors.

Strategy Challenged MSCI’s Operating-Business Test

During consultation, Strategy’s challenge to MSCI’s classification alleged that the approach targeted digital asset treasury companies. It argued that the methodology repackaged a withdrawn 2025 proposal aimed at firms with digital assets worth at least half their total assets. The company urged MSCI to withdraw the test.

Its defense centered on a bitcoin treasury business it reported as an operating segment under U.S. accounting standards. Strategy maintained that MSCI’s operating and non-operating terminology lacked a basis in recognized accounting frameworks. It also argued that the methodology inserted policy judgments into index construction.

In its public consultation response, the company said exclusion would not meaningfully affect its business. MSCI-linked funds then held approximately 13 million shares, equivalent to 3.1% of Strategy’s basic shares outstanding. The company put that holding at 60% of its 30-day average daily trading volume, less than one day’s turnover.

title: MSCI Removes Strategy (MSTR) From Its USA Index, Forcing Index Funds to Sell by Nov. 30
summary:
Bitcoin Magazine

MSCI Removes Strategy (MSTR) From Its USA Index, Forcing Index Funds to Sell by Nov. 30
MSCI will take Strategy, Metaplanet, Yellow Cake, Skel and Upexi out of its global indexes as of the Nov. 30 close, after a new screen classified them as non-operating companies.
This post MSCI ...
content:
MSCI will remove Strategy, the largest corporate bitcoin holder, from the MSCI USA Index as of the close of Nov. 30, the index provider said Wednesday, after a new screen classified the company as a non-operating issuer.

The decision is part of MSCI’s November 2026 Index Review, posted shortly after 5 p.m. ET. Official additions and deletions lists show Strategy (MSTR) out of its USA Index, which also takes it out of the broader MSCI World and ACWI indexes. The same review deletes Japan’s Metaplanet from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index and uranium holder Yellow Cake from the MSCI United Kingdom Small Cap Index, and it removes Iceland’s Skel Fjárfestingafélag from the MSCI Iceland Frontier Markets Small Cap Index and micro-cap Upexi from the USA Micro Cap Index. All five had already been marked Deleted on MSCI’s potential-impact list, built on Sept. 30 financial data and Oct. 9 market values.

Strategy is the only large-cap name in the group and, on that October list, accounted for more than 90% of the five companies’ combined float-adjusted market value. The company held 850,364 bitcoin as of Nov. 8, acquired at an average price of $75,456 a coin, or $64.16 billion in aggregate.

Strategy shares closed at $122.35, up 1.06%, then slipped 1.51% to $120.50 in after-hours trading as of 5:34 p.m. ET.

How the MSCI screen works

The rule does not mention bitcoin. The index first checks whether a company’s operating assets equal at least 50% of total assets. Issuers that fail that core screen face five financial ratios, and a company flagged on four or more of them is ineligible for the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes.

Buffers limit turnover. A company outside the indexes cannot be added if it fails the ineligibility screen in either of its two most recent annual filing periods, but a current constituent is removed only if it fails in each of them. The index said it may also use the most recent interim filing.

MSCI also said Wednesday that the same non-operating treatment will apply to the MSCI US Index Series.

The screen replaces an approach aimed squarely at crypto. The index first proposed in late 2025 to exclude companies whose digital assets made up 50% or more of total assets, then dropped that plan in January and opened a broader consultation in August. It adopted the new methodology on Oct. 15, with minor modifications, and said it would end the interim measures it had placed on those companies in October 2025, including a freeze on share-count increases and a deferral of additions.

What the deletion does and does not do

Funds that track an MSCI index have to hold what the index holds, so they will have to sell the deleted stocks by the Nov. 30 close. JPMorgan analysts estimated last November that an exclusion could drive about $2.8 billion of outflows from Strategy, and as much as $8.8 billion more if other index providers followed. That estimate was built on MSCI’s earlier digital-asset proposal, not the October screen, and MSCI itself has published no figure.

A removal does not delist Strategy’s stock, and nothing in the rules forces the company to sell bitcoin. The pressure lands on the shares, and through them on the premium Strategy uses to fund new purchases by selling stock.

In an August letter, the company said a deletion “would have no meaningful impact on Strategy’s business.” Strategy has also said funds tracking MSCI’s global investable indexes hold 3.1% of its basic shares outstanding, and that it reports its bitcoin treasury as an operating segment under U.S. GAAP.

Seventeen other constituents were on the potential watchlist, including SharpLink, TON Strategy and Solana Company. Those names do not appear among Wednesday’s published deletions.

Tokyo-listed Metaplanet is the other bitcoin treasury firm in the deleted group, after it sold bitcoin last quarter to show investors it could tap its holdings for liquidity. Strategy bought 1,036 bitcoin for $81.9 million in the week to Nov. 8, a purchase that left its holdings below that average cost.

Micah Zimmerman

Micah first discovered Bitcoin in 2018 but remained a skeptic on the sidelines for too long. Since 2021, he has covered crypto and business and now works as a news reporter for Bitcoin Magazine, based in North Carolina.

title: Suiet wallet to shut down in latest exit from Sui ecosystem
summary: The self-custodial wallet will keep its API services running through Nov. 14. Sui’s DeFi total value locked has fallen more than 22% over the past month.
content:
Cryptocurrency wallet Suiet is shutting down, adding to a series of closures and service withdrawals in the Sui ecosystem.

Suiet, a self-custodial wallet built for the Sui blockchain, said in a notice that it will stop updating and supporting its wallet, with API services set to end after Nov. 14. The shutdown comes as the Sui network has seen a sharp decline in decentralized finance (DeFi) activity.

Sui’s total value locked (TVL) stood at about $413 million on Wednesday, down more than 22% over the past month, according to DefiLlama data. Data from Token Terminal shows that Sui averaged about 128,000 daily active users in October, down from 601,000 in November 2025 – or around a 79% drop.

Meanwhile, other recent closures have also raised concerns about the costs and challenges of keeping projects running on the Sui network.

“Sui’s problems seem to mostly be of an economic nature resulting from expensive engineering costs and low user volume rather than protocol failures,” Kadan Stadelmann, former chief technology officer of Komodo Platform, told Cointelegraph. “No flaw in the system’s core design has been found.”

Cointelegraph reached out to the Sui Foundation and Suiet for comment but had not received responses by publication.

Related: Sui DeFi protocol Full Sail to wind down after Switchboard incident

Recent closures and departures

Suiet’s shutdown immediately follows the Sui-based hardware wallet project Suiball also announcing its closure on Nov. 10. Meanwhile wallet provider Phantom ended support for Sui in September.

DeFi project Full Sail also shut down following a security incident involving Switchboard that caused about $91,000 in losses.

Despite the decline in active users, transactions on Sui have increased, reaching 324 million in October, up from 101 million in November 2025, according to Token Terminal. However, more transactions do not necessarily mean more users, and wallet providers must still decide whether supporting the network is worth the cost, according to Stadelmann.

“Multi-chain wallets have expansive attack surfaces, and Sui’s approach adds costs for vendors who can take their business to less capital intensive chains,” he said. “Any individual failure of a multi-chain wallet is more a reflection of the risks rather than an indictment of any given protocol.”

A series of outages

Sui has also experienced four network outages in 2026, resulting in around 22 hours of combined downtime, according to reports published by the Sui Foundation.

The network stopped processing transactions for about six hours in January, followed by three more outages on May 28 and 29. The May disruptions were linked to software bugs, including problems introduced by a network update, the Sui Foundation said at the time.

By comparison, rival blockchain Solana has not recorded a network-wide outage since February 2024, when it went offline for nearly five hours. Meanwhile, Aptos, which uses the same underlying smart contract programming language as Sui, last reported a mainnet outage in October 2023.

Network outages are significant because they can prevent DeFi users from trading, transferring funds or managing positions, although the Sui Foundation said no user funds were at risk during its May disruptions.

title: What Is Binance Pay and How to Find Its ID?
summary:
Binance Pay is a contactless, secure, and borderless means of sending and receiving crypto payments within the Binance platform. You can pay, receive, and send crypto with no fees at
The post What Is Binance Pay and How to Find Its ID? appeared first on CryptoNinjas.
content:
Binance Pay is a contactless, secure, and borderless means of sending and receiving crypto payments within the Binance platform. You can pay, receive, and send crypto with no fees at all, straight from your Binance account. You don’t have to copy lengthy wallet addresses or concern yourself with selecting the correct blockchain network. It all takes place within the Binance app, so crypto transfers are fast and hassle-free.

The benefits of using Binance Pay are simple. It is free to use, with no network fees or gas fees. Transactions are instant, so you don’t have to wait for confirmations. It also works globally, which means you can send and receive crypto from people around the world who use Binance. Plus, it’s safe and backed by Binance’s security system.

This guide will explain what Binance Pay is, how it works, and provide a step-by-step guide on how to use Binance Pay. You’ll learn how to create a Binance account and how to send and receive crypto with Binance Pay.

  • What Is Binance Pay?
    • What Are the Pros and Cons of Binance Pay?
      • Who Can Use Binance Pay?
    • What Is Binance Pay Merchant?
      • What Are the Benefits of a Binance Merchant Account?
  • How Binance Pay Works?
    • What Are the Fees of Binance Pay?
    • Is Binance Pay Safe?
  • How to Use Binance Pay?
    • How to Register a New Account on Binance to Use Binance Pay?
    • How to Send and Receive Crypto With Binance Pay?
      • Can You Pay Someone on Binance?
    • What Is Binance Pay ID?
      • Where to Find Binance Pay ID?
      • Is Binance Pay Legal in India?

What Is Binance Pay?

Binance Pay is a feature that allows you to send and receive crypto instantly and free of charge. You can use it to pay your friends, send money to relatives, or accept payments for your business. It is very easy to use and operates within the Binance app. Binance Pay accepts more than 100 cryptocurrencies for payments, and you can make payments using coins such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, USDC, and BNB. Also, you can select which coin you wish to use first when you are making a payment. Binance Pay also works as a Binance payment gateway that helps businesses accept crypto payments easily.

Currently, Binance Pay has more than 40 million active users, and most of the individuals use it to spend their cryptocurrency at tens of thousands of stores, both online and offline. You can use it to shop, pay for food, book travel, and more. It also works well for sending money across countries, and even it is much faster than a bank transfer and has zero fees.

To use it, first, you require a Binance account, and after logging in, proceed to the Binance Pay option on the app. You can send cryptocurrency by using an individual’s Pay ID, phone number, or email. You can also scan their QR code, and the cryptocurrency will be sent to their Pay wallet immediately.

Start using Binance Pay today to send and receive crypto instantly, securely, and with zero fees – no wallet addresses or networks needed, just smooth and easy payments.

What Are the Pros and Cons of Binance Pay?

Pros of Binance Pay

The pros of using Binance Pay are easy to use, low fees, global transactions, secure payments, and flexible payment features.

  • Easy to Use: Binance Pay makes it easy for you to send or receive cryptocurrency with only a couple of taps on your phone. You can quickly pay merchants or share bills with your friends. It supports more than 100 cryptocurrencies, and that means you have lots of cryptocurrency alternatives.
  • Low or No Charges: The majority of Binance Pay transactions are completely free, and that’s great for keeping costs down. But, for larger transactions, above 140,000 USDT, you need to pay 1 USDT. That’s really not expensive compared to using old-style payment methods. You can also view all the charges before finalizing the transaction.
  • Global Reach: You can send crypto anywhere in the world instantly and with low fees. International transfers from traditional banks take days or even weeks. Binance Pay does it instantly, and it’s best for paying friends or shopping around the world.
  • Secure Payments: Binance Pay has robust security features, such as two-factor authentication and encryption. This protects your funds and information. Also, Binance has a good history of safeguarding users. You can rely on it for daily payments.
  • Flexible Features: You can easily modify the way you spend your crypto or even send crypto gift boxes. It is also capable of mobile top-ups and peer-to-peer transfers.

Cons of Binance Pay

The cons of using Binance Pay are mandatory KYC verification, limited acceptance by merchants, customer support delays, and regulatory risks.

  • Requires KYC Verification: You need to go through extra Binance Know Your Customer procedures to use it. You have to provide personal information, such as your ID and address. Some find this restrictive on privacy grounds.
  • Limited Acceptance by Merchants: Few retailers currently accept Binance Pay. You can use it on Binance’s Marketplace, but there is limited choice. Of course, adoption is increasing, but it’s not quite there yet.
  • Customer Support Problems: Binance’s customer service is not always good. When you encounter issues, such as a failed transaction, it may take some time before you can receive assistance. It can be irritating when you urgently need fixes to be done immediately.
  • Regulatory Risks: As you know, crypto payments are subject to uncertain regulations in certain nations. Binance has experienced legal troubles previously that may influence Binance Pay. So, this creates some risk when using it for the long term.

Who Can Use Binance Pay?

You can use Binance Pay if you want to send payments, a shopper or traveler, a business wishing to accept crypto, an individual who wishes to send gifts, or wishes to handle automated subscriptions.

  • People who want to send payments: Any person with a verified Binance account can easily send crypto to friends or relatives around the globe. All you need is the recipient’s Binance ID, email address, or phone number, or you can scan their QR code too. It’s quick, often free, and supports more than 100 cryptocurrencies.
  • Shoppers and travelers: Binance Pay allows you to purchase items or book travel with cryptocurrency at thousands of online and offline retailers. Here, you can pay for clothes, electronics, or even hotel nights on websites like Travala. It supports more than 100 different cryptocurrencies, so you have many options. So, it’s great for anyone who wants to spend crypto as easily as cash.
  • Businesses wishing to accept crypto: Merchants can accept payments in crypto from users on Binance. They must apply for a merchant account with Binance Pay. They can also process payments and refunds via the Merchant Management Platform.
  • People who want to send gifts: You can use the Binance Pay Red Packet function to send cryptocurrency gifts. You have to select the token, value, and number of recipients. The recipient will receive a random amount until all funds are claimed.
  • People who want to handle subscriptions: Binance Pay supports recurring payments. This is very helpful for individuals who wish to manage subscriptions or pay regularly. You can easily approve repeated payments to merchants.

What Is Binance Pay Merchant?

A Binance Pay merchant is a business or individual who accepts crypto payments from customers using Binance Pay. It is easy to do. You simply need to register, get verified, and use tools such as QR codes or payment links to receive payments. 

Simply, customers have to scan or click to pay with cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin or USDT instantly. You can use stablecoins such as USDT to prevent crypto price fluctuations. It also supports all types of businesses, such as stores, cafes, or online platforms. You can manage everything via the Merchant Management Platform, including monitoring payments, handling refunds, and withdrawing funds.

What Are the Benefits of a Binance Merchant Account?

The benefits of a Binance Merchant Account are low transaction fees, access to a huge customer base, fast and secure payments, and easy setup and management. 

  • Low or No Transaction Fees: You can create a free Binance Merchant Account, and you will also often pay little to no fees for crypto transactions. This is better compared to traditional payment methods like credit cards, which nowadays charge very high fees. It also helps small businesses save money, and you can keep more of your profits. Plus, payments settle instantly, which is great for cash flow as a business.
  • Access to a Huge Customer Base: Binance has over 250 million users worldwide on its centralized crypto exchange, and there are 40 million active Binance Pay users. As a merchant, you can tap into this massive audience and take your chance to attract crypto fans who prefer paying with Bitcoin or USDT. This can boost your sales, and you can reach customers globally without dealing with currency exchange hassles.
  • Fast and Secure Payments: Crypto payments through Binance Pay are quick and safe. Transactions happen instantly, so you don’t have to wait days for your funds. The best part, the blockchain technology keeps things secure and reduces fraud risks. 
  • Easy Setup and Management: Setting up a Binance Merchant Account is super simple. You just need to sign up, get verified, and start accepting payments fast. The Merchant Management Platform also lets you track payments, issue refunds, and withdraw funds easily. You can even integrate it with your website or app without much technical knowledge. Hence, it’s user-friendly even for small businesses.

Try Binance Pay now and enjoy fast, fee-free crypto transfers worldwide – perfect for paying friends, shopping online, or accepting payments with just a tap.

How Binance Pay Works?

Binance Pay works as a contactless and safe method for paying and receiving crypto. It enables you to make payments or transfer currencies without sharing personal information. It is developed within the Binance app itself, therefore, you don’t have to install anything additional apps or extensions.

Here’s how it works. Firstly, you sign up for a Binance account. Next, you need to create your Binance Pay account. From there, you can send and receive crypto. To send, you simply need to use someone’s Binance Pay ID, phone number, email address, or QR code. The recipient will receive it instantly in their Binance Pay account.

Here, the platform is using internal transfers. So, when you transfer using Binance Pay, the transfer does not occur on the blockchain. It occurs within the Binance system. It is therefore instant and charges zero fees. Also, you don’t need to hold crypto in a different Pay wallet. The system will use the amount from your Binance exchange funding wallet.

What Are the Fees of Binance Pay?

Binance Pay is free of charge for individual transfers. It does not cost you any additional fee when you send cryptocurrency directly to an individual with the help of Binance Pay. There is no transaction fee for internal transfers on the platform. Receiving is free of charge as well. If someone pays you using crypto with the use of Binance Pay, you receive your full amount.

Now, there may be fees if you use other Binance Pay services. For instance, if you make a purchase from a vendor and the transaction entails currency conversion, Binance will implement its standard conversion spread. This is not an explicit fee, but the exchange rate you receive may differ slightly from the market rate. This is also called a spread fee.

For merchants, Binance introduced a rule where mini-program merchants need to hit a minimum transaction volume, or they’ll pay a quarterly fee. Also, Binance Payouts have a fee of 0.80% per transaction, capped at $5 or equivalent. All fees are shown upfront before you confirm a payment, so there are no surprises. Refunds, if they happen, go back to your Binance Pay Wallet in USDT.

Is Binance Pay Safe?

Yes, Binance Pay is safe as it is built on Binance Exchange’s secure system. It applies Binance’s robust security measures to safeguard your account and funds. First of all, the platform employs two-factor authentication (2FA). To access Binance Pay, you must enable it. This adds an extra layer of protection, requiring a code from your phone in combination with your password.

It also includes device management. This allows you to view the devices logged into your account. If you find an unknown device logged into your account, you can remove it to protect your account. The platform also uses anti-phishing codes. If you receive an email from Binance, the code is displayed in the email, ensuring you won’t receive a fraudulent email.

Binance Pay operates within the Binance environment. Therefore, it employs the same security tools as the rest of the Binance exchange. These tools include cold storage of user balances, risk monitoring, and smart internal controls.

Additionally, Binance Pay payments are internal transfers. They do not go onto public blockchains, which reduces the risk of external attacks. You also do not reveal your wallet address when making a payment. Binance monitors for suspicious activity using risk systems and artificial intelligence. If something seems wrong, your account is frozen to prevent fraud. Your personal information and payment details are also encrypted. You do not share either your payment history or your personal information with the other individual.

Send and receive crypto anytime, anywhere using Binance Pay – easy to use, no hidden fees, and fully integrated with your Binance wallet for fast payments.

How to Use Binance Pay?

To use Binance Pay, you need a verified Binance account. First, open your Binance app and log in. Tap on the “Pay” icon on the home screen. Now you can send or receive crypto with just a few taps. You can also scan another person’s Binance Pay QR code or share your own.

How to Register a New Account on Binance to Use Binance Pay?

To register a new Binance account, follow these three steps: sign up with your email or phone number, verify your identity (KYC), and activate Binance Pay.

Step 1: Sign Up with Your Email or Phone Number

Go to binance.com or download the Binance app from the App Store or Google Play Store. On the site, click the yellow “Sign Up” button at the top right. In the app, tap the icon at the bottom right and choose “Sign Up.” Enter your email or telephone number and use a secure password (blending letters, numbers, and characters for security). Here, you can also use our Binance referral code to get a $100 welcome bonus. Now, a confirmation code will be sent to your email or phone – check your messages or inbox and enter the code to confirm. This takes only a moment or two and sets up your account.

Join millions of users already using Binance Pay and make instant crypto payments with ease, skip the fees, and enjoy a smooth and secure transaction every time.

To secure your account, turn on 2FA immediately after you create an account. On the website, you must click your account icon and then “Settings.” You can use Google Authenticator, SMS, or email for 2FA. With Google Authenticator, you need to download the app, scan the QR code that Binance gives you, and save the backup key somewhere secure. With SMS or email, you receive codes on your phone or inbox for logins and transactions. It’s a five-minute step, but one that’s well worth it for peace of mind.

Step 2: Complete Identity Verification (KYC)

Binance requires identity verification for compliance purposes and to enable features like Binance Pay. On the website, click your profile icon and go to “Verification.” You will be required to upload an official government-issued document, such as a passport, driver’s license, or national identity card, and an address verification, for example, a bill or bank statement. 

Sometimes, Binance will request a selfie or a rapid face scan using the camera on your device. This is an easy procedure, and Binance will likely have it processed within a few minutes, but it may take a couple of days when it’s during peak hours. This step secures your account and prepares it for most features on Binance Pay.

Step 3: Activate Binance Pay

After your account has been verified, enable Binance Pay. Go to “More” in the primary menu and choose “Pay”. Pick a special nickname for anonymity (like “CryptoNinja” instead of your actual name) and enter a six-digit Pay PIN for secure payments. 

Accept the terms and conditions and click “Activate.” This connects your account to Binance Pay, and you can start sending and receiving crypto immediately. The entire process takes only a minute or two, and you’re live.

How to Send and Receive Crypto With Binance Pay?

To send and receive crypto with Binance Pay, follow these steps: funding your wallet, sending crypto via QR code or contact details, and receiving crypto by sharing your QR code or Binance ID.

Step 1: Fund your Binance Wallet

Before sending cryptocurrency, confirm your Binance Funding Wallet has a balance. Click the “Wallets” icon at the top, then “Overview.” Alternatively, you can buy some if you don’t have cryptocurrency, using a bank transfer, credit card, or P2P trade. 

To purchase, click “Buy Crypto” on the landing page, select your fiat currency (e.g., USD or EUR), and pick a cryptocurrency like Bitcoin or USDT. Follow directions to finalize the purchase, which will take a few minutes. You can also move your cryptocurrency from another wallet or exchange to your Binance Funding Wallet by copying your wallet address (found under “Wallets” > “Overview” > “Deposit”). With funding, your cryptocurrency is now prepared for use through Binance Pay.

Step 2: Send Crypto through QR Code or Contact Information

Launch the Binance app and click the “Pay” icon on the home screen. Click “Send,” then pick how you send, either scan the recipient’s Binance QR code or enter the recipient’s details by email, mobile number, or Binance Pay ID. To scan using the QR code scanner, tap the scan icon on the home screen or long-press the icon on the home screen. 

To enter contact details, enter or paste the recipient’s details and click “Continue.” Pick the cryptocurrency, enter the amount, and add an optional message (e.g., “Lunch money”). Double-check, click “Confirm,” and enter your Pay PIN or complete 2-step verification. The transfer is instantaneous, but double-check it; ultimately, sending to the wrong details is irreversible.

Step 3: Receive Crypto by Sharing QR Code or Binance ID 

To get crypto, navigate to the “Pay” tab within the app and click “Receive.” A QR code will appear; share it by saving the image or sending it through WhatsApp, email, or other apps. For a desired amount of crypto, click “Set Currency/Amount,” select the coin (e.g., BNB or ETH), enter the desired amount, and add a comment if you prefer. Click “Confirm” to create a one-off QR code. 

Alternatively, you can share your Binance account email, phone number, or your Binance ID (in “User Center”). After the payer makes the payment, the crypto ends up directly in your Funding Wallet, and you’ll be notified by email or SMS.

Can You Pay Someone on Binance?

Yes, you can pay someone on Binance using Binance Pay. You just need their Pay ID, email, phone number, or you can scan their Binance Pay QR code. Open the Binance app, tap on “Pay,” choose “Send,” and enter their details. Select the crypto you want to send, enter the amount, and tap “Confirm.” The payment will be sent instantly with no fees. Both you and the person must have Binance accounts to use this feature. You can also read our in-depth Binance review to get full information about the exchange.

What Is Binance Pay ID?

Binance Pay ID is a special numerical code that Binance automatically assigns to your account when you enable Binance Pay. It is an individual code that allows other Binance members to send you cryptocurrency directly into the Binance Pay system. You cannot change or personalize your Pay ID like a username or email address. Your Pay ID is generated by Binance and is tied to your account specifically.

Use Binance Pay to handle all your crypto transfers in one place with no fees, fast delivery, and a smooth experience every time you send or receive funds.

Where to Find Binance Pay ID?

To find your Binance Pay ID, log in to your Binance account via the mobile app or website. Now, you need to navigate to the “Pay” section, where your Pay ID will be displayed along with a corresponding QR code. You can share this Pay ID with others who wish to send you crypto, as this provides a straightforward and secure method for transactions within the Binance ecosystem.

Is Binance Pay Legal in India?

Yes, Binance Pay is legal for use in India as of 2025. Binance has formally registered with the Financial Intelligence Unit of India (FIU-IND), enabling it to operate lawfully by being compliant with local laws, particularly anti-money laundering (AML) regulations. This registration enables Indian users to access Binance services, such as Binance Pay, as long as they undergo the required Know Your Customer (KYC) verification procedure.

title: Bitcoin Core Discloses High-Severity Security Bug That Could Halt Mining Nodes
summary: Bitcoin Core disclosed three security vulnerabilities on Nov. 10, 2026, including a high-severity defect capable of disrupting mining operations and two additional weaknesses affecting block processing and Tor connections. Although developers patched the problems in October 2025, their technical det...
content:
Bitcoin Core disclosed three security vulnerabilities on Nov. 10, 2026, including a high-severity defect capable of disrupting mining operations and two additional weaknesses affecting block processing and Tor connections. Although developers patched the problems in October 2025, their technical details remained confidential until now.

Key Takeaways

  • Bitcoin Core disclosed three previously patched vulnerabilities this week, including one capable of interrupting mining operations.
  • The most serious defect could prevent affected nodes from producing valid block templates following a blockchain reorganization.
  • Thousands of nodes faced potential exposure to a separate Tor configuration flaw, although default installations were unaffected.

How Could a Bitcoin Core Bug Bring Mining Operations to a Halt?

The most consequential vulnerability, identified as CVE-2025-62861, affected Bitcoin Core versions 28.0 through 28.2 and 29.0 through 29.1. Classified as high severity, the defect involved transaction handling during blockchain reorganizations, potentially leaving mining nodes unable to construct valid block templates.

At its center were version 3 transactions, commonly called TRUC transactions, which operate under specialized mempool restrictions. During a chain reorganization, Bitcoin Core could incorrectly evict transactions while retaining dependent transactions, creating inconsistencies within its transaction pool.

For miners, the consequences were particularly troublesome. Affected nodes could fail block template validation, effectively preventing them from generating fresh mining work until restarted. Mining equipment could continue hashing outdated templates, potentially forfeiting transaction fees and reducing operational efficiency.

Security researcher Niklas Goegge reported the defect on Sept. 26, 2025. Developer Greg Sanders subsequently introduced a correction, merged Oct. 2, that prevented the problematic transaction eviction behavior during reorganizations.

The remedy appeared in the software Bitcoin Core 30.0, 29.2, and 28.3 throughout October 2025. Nevertheless, approximately 9% of reachable nodes continued advertising vulnerable versions around the disclosure date.

What Were the Other Two Bitcoin Core Security Vulnerabilities?

The second vulnerability, CVE-2025-62859, carried a medium-severity classification and involved maliciously constructed compact blocks. An attacker could exploit improper handling of altered transaction witnesses to repeatedly delay block downloads. Under particular network conditions, including compromised high-bandwidth peer connections, the interference could continue indefinitely.

Researcher Eugene Siegel identified the weakness in April 2025. Gregory Sanders developed the correction, which reached Bitcoin Core versions 30.0 and 29.2.

Meanwhile, CVE-2025-62860 exposed an entirely different problem involving inbound Tor connections and trusted-peer permissions. When operators configured Bitcoin Core’s optional -whitelist setting to include their Tor daemon’s address, incoming connections could mistakenly inherit privileges intended for trusted peers.

Those exemptions weakened certain denial-of-service safeguards and privacy protections. Bitcoin Core indicated that thousands of reachable mainnet nodes were potentially affected, although standard configurations remained safe.

Why Did Bitcoin Core Wait Until November to Disclose the Flaws?

The Nov. 10 announcements followed Bitcoin Core’s established disclosure schedule. Developers withheld technical details until the final vulnerable major release line, 29.x, reached end-of-life status on Oct. 27, 2026. Unlike three AI-assisted vulnerability disclosures published Oct. 28, these issues followed the conventional embargo process.

Importantly, none permitted any bitcoin theft, unauthorized coin creation, or consensus failure, and no exploitation was reported. The mining vulnerability required specific reorganization conditions, meaning its consequences were confined to affected operators rather than Bitcoin itself.

For bitcoin miners and node administrators, the distinction matters. Software maintenance remains essential even when vulnerabilities cannot compromise funds. The episode illustrates how seemingly obscure transaction-handling defects can create tangible operational problems without threatening the network’s underlying consensus.

title: Nvidia preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang after affairs: WSJ
summary: The report about Huang’s possible departure came after the New York Times reported that he had a second extramarital affair.
content:
Nvidia’s board is preparing to oust founder and CEO Jensen Huang after he had two extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reported.

Directors could meet as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future, the report said, citing people familiar with the matter.

His potential removal would mark a major leadership change for the chipmaker, which has become central to the artificial intelligence boom under Huang.

Cointelegraph reached out to Nvidia for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

One affair involved Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. US intelligence officials believe she was a spy for Beijing.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an extramarital affair with Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to five people who worked at the company.

On Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a letter to employees, apologizing for breaching their trust.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did,” he wrote.

Huang also confirmed that Nvidia’s board had launched an independent investigation into national security concerns raised in news reports. He pledged to cooperate fully and said he remained committed to the company.

Nvidia shares fell 8% to $159.76 in after-hours trading following the reports, reversing a 2.9% gain during the regular session, according to Google Finance data.

Related: BTC price eyes $73K amid Nvidia volatility: Three things to know in Bitcoin this week

title: Here’s what happened in crypto today
summary: Need to know what happened in crypto today? Here is the latest news on daily trends and events impacting Bitcoin price, blockchain, DeFi, Web3 and crypto regulation.
content:
Today in crypto, OKX and Intercontinental Exchange are preparing to launch tokenized stock trading on Nov. 23 despite objections from major companies, Barclays increased its holdings in BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF by 48% in the third quarter, and pro-crypto lawmaker Tom Emmer was elected House Republican minority whip as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.

OKXICE moves ahead with tokenized stocks as blue chips push back

Crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) are set to launch tokenized stock trading on Nov. 23, despite objections from 67 companies to having their shares listed and warnings from Nasdaq that trading across disconnected platforms could fragment liquidity.

The venture, known as OKXICE, will operate under the US Securities and Exchange Commission’s temporary Innovation Exemption and offer eligible US customers round-the-clock trading. Under the exemption, venues must give companies a chance to object before listing shares tokenized by an unaffiliated third party. JPMorgan Chase, McDonald’s, SpaceX and Coca-Cola were among the companies that objected. 

Tokenized stocks are blockchain-based tokens that represent company shares or track their price. The rights they carry depend on how they are structured. The distributed value of tokenized stocks and ETFs reached $3.88 billion on Nov. 11, up 13.4% over 30 days. 

In comments to Cointelegraph, former New York governor and OKXICE co-chair Andrew Cuomo said investors would have “the same rights, protections and ownership that come with the underlying shares.” 

Barclays boosts BlackRock Bitcoin ETF stake 48% as banks expand holdings

Barclays reported holding 3.94 million shares in BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin exchange-traded fund (ETF) at the end of the third quarter, up 48% from the previous quarter.

The position in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) was worth about $187 million on Sept. 30, up from $88.5 million for 2.66 million shares on June 30, according to Barclays’ Friday Form 13F filing.

“Early readings suggest longer-term holders make up a growing share of the spot bitcoin ETF investor base,” Bitwise analyst Camran Khosravi told Cointelegraph, pointing to increased bank exposure, including at Citigroup.

Citigroup reported a new position worth about $119 million in the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC). Its reported IBIT holdings also rose 50% to about 521,000 shares, from 347,000 at the end of June.

The filings offer an early indication of changing institutional Bitcoin ETF ownership, with more major banks and hedge funds yet to disclose their third-quarter positions. Institutional investment managers have until Monday to file their third-quarter holdings reports.

Crypto ally Tom Emmer elected House GOP minority whip

Pro-crypto US Representative Tom Emmer has been elected House Republican minority whip, securing the party’s second-highest leadership position as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January.

Emmer beat Texas Representative August Pfluger in a 103-76 secret ballot vote, according to Politico. He previously served as House Republican majority whip and will remain the party’s No. 2 leader, this time under incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan.

As minority whip, Emmer will be responsible for rallying Republican votes, coordinating the party’s legislative strategy and helping maintain unity on key bills.

“Tom has been one of the strongest advocates for digital assets in Congress, and he has led the fight against a government-controlled CBDC and stood up for American innovators,” GOP Senator Cynthia Lummis said on X.

title: Uncalled US House races could send more crypto allies to Congress
summary: The remaining races feature pro-crypto candidates and others without a stated position, giving advocacy groups what they see as “an opportunity” for outreach.
content:
Just over a week after a “blue wave” handed Democrats control of the US House and Senate, 14 races have yet to be called. The results so far have added crypto supporters in both chambers and the remaining races could bring more into Congress.

Three candidates in the uncalled races received backing from crypto political action committees (PACs). According to Stand With Crypto, every candidate in those races is either strongly pro-crypto or has no stated position.

As crypto advocacy groups look ahead to 2028, they’re turning their attention to candidates who have yet to take a public stance on crypto.

House races still to be called

Crypto PACs backed three candidates in US House races that remain undecided. Two incumbents lead in Alaska and North Carolina, while a Louisiana state senator faces a December runoff.

Rep. Nick Begich leads in Alaska’s US House race. Defend American Jobs, Fairshake’s Republican-facing affiliate, backed him with $508,142 in the August primary. The same PAC put $150,600 behind Rep. David Rouzer, who leads in North Carolina’s 7th District.

Louisiana state Sen. Blake Miguez will face Democrat Chauna Banks in a Dec. 12 runoff for the state’s 6th District. The Fellowship PAC backed Miguez with $250,000.

The Associated Press called the race in South Carolina’s 2nd District for incumbent Rep. Joe Wilson on the morning of Nov. 11. Stand With Crypto rates Wilson as “strongly supportive of crypto.” His win brought the group’s House tally to 246 crypto supporters and 107 opponents, while the Senate stood at 50 supporters and 33 opponents.

In the remaining races, Stand With Crypto lists each candidate as either strongly supportive of crypto or having no stated position. “The new members that have no stance present an opportunity,” Blockchain Association Chief Policy Officer Lindsay Fraser told Cointelegraph.

Educating the incoming congress

Nearly one in four members of the incoming Congress will be new, Fraser said, and many have given little thought to blockchain technology. “To us, that represents a blank slate in terms of education,” she said.

Blockchain Association is planning a January fly-in to reach newly elected lawmakers. “Leaving the 120th Congress with more members in that A and B category would be a huge success,” she said, referring to Stand With Crypto’s ratings. The group gives an A to candidates who strongly support crypto and a B to those who are somewhat supportive.

Fraser said age plays a bigger role than party affiliation in how lawmakers vote on crypto. She said members under 55 are much more likely to support the industry and that the incoming class skews younger.

Fraser said she wants the industry to enter the 2028 election “with two candidates who […] are thoughtful in regards to the industry,” so the sector can avoid “living and dying by the outcome of that election.”

title: From Prison Cell to $2.7M Crypto Heist, Scottish Criminal Gets 8 More Years
summary: A Scottish prisoner who masterminded an elaborate £2 million cryptocurrency robbery from behind bars has received another eight years in prison. The audacious scheme combined sophisticated cybercrime with an old-fashioned home invasion, but ultimately collapsed when the intended victims refused to o...
content:
A Scottish prisoner who masterminded an elaborate £2 million cryptocurrency robbery from behind bars has received another eight years in prison. The audacious scheme combined sophisticated cybercrime with an old-fashioned home invasion, but ultimately collapsed when the intended victims refused to open their door.

Key Takeaways

  • A £2 million crypto fortune ($2.7M), illicit prison communications, and a carefully orchestrated robbery converged in an unusual Scottish criminal case.
  • Investigators uncovered months of planning, including surveillance, secret messages, and preparations for a potentially violent confrontation.
  • A failed burglary and a late-night encounter ultimately exposed the limitations of an otherwise elaborate criminal operation.

Prison Cell Becomes Command Center for £2 Million Cryptocurrency Plot

On Nov. 10, 2026, Lord Cubie sentenced 29-year-old Robert Barr at the High Court in Glasgow, alongside accomplices Sean Favier, 26, and Iain Doyle, 37. According to the official sentencing statement published by Scotland’s judiciary, all three pleaded guilty to involvement in serious organized crime. Barr received eight years, Favier four years, and Doyle five years.

Lord Cubie characterized the operation as a crime that “married 21st century computer sophistication with old fashioned housebreaking in an audacious attempt to steal cryptocurrency worth up to £2 million.” The scheme targeted a couple in Bonnyrigg, Midlothian, whose cryptocurrency holdings included assets associated with a digital currency venture.

Already imprisoned for cryptocurrency-related fraud, Barr allegedly coordinated the operation through illicit mobile phones. His accomplices were supposed to enter the victims’ residence and compel them to install AnyDesk, a legitimate remote-access application.

The judge explained the intended mechanics:

“Having control of the couple’s computer, he would input the receiving cryptocurrency address and transfer the cryptocurrency from the couple’s wallet to other accounts in his control, thus taking the value of the cryptocurrency for his own use.”

Investigators recovered extensive communications from Barr’s phone, documenting reconnaissance, surveillance, and discussions contemplating intimidation or violence.

One message demanded:

“WHEN THEY’RE IN HIS HOUSE GONNA NEED GET HIM ON TO HIS PC FAST N DOWNLOAD ANYDESK RAPID”

An earlier burglary in January 2024 produced a stolen hardware wallet, but the perpetrators could not access the crypto assets. The subsequent attempt unfolded around 11:30 p.m. on April 17, 2024, when Favier and Doyle approached the property wearing dark clothing with their faces concealed. The couple spotted them through a doorbell camera and refused entry.

Lord Cubie observed that the operation was “only frustrated because the victims had the sense not to open their front door at 11:30 p.m. at night to unknown men, dressed in dark clothing with their faces obscured.” The case comes as home invasions and so-called wrench attacks against crypto investors have been on the rise.

Judge Rejects Barr’s Defense as Criminal Mastermind Faces Further Prison Time

During sentencing, Lord Cubie dismissed Barr’s suggestion that he had been “easily led,” pointing instead to his leadership and considerable technical capabilities.

The judge stated:

“You have accepted in the narrative being the head of the organized crime group which carried out the offense and are described as a sophisticated cybercriminal with the ability to orchestrate a level of criminality rarely seen within mainstream investigations.”

Addressing Barr directly, he added:

“Your culpability is high.”

The court also considered Barr’s previous cryptocurrency fraud conviction and his willingness to organize another offense while incarcerated. Regarding Doyle, the judge rejected his claim that he merely intended to deliver a telephone, noting his awareness of potential violence. Favier’s participation was considered comparatively peripheral.

Although neither attempted theft succeeded, Lord Cubie stressed the seriousness of the criminal enterprise.

“This was a serious crime, a pre-planned and meaningful, although ultimately unsuccessful, attempt to steal a substantial asset which involved the invasion of the home of the victims, a real potential for violence, and if successful, material assistance in the financing of serious and organized crime,” the sentencing letter states.

Barr’s sentence runs from Aug. 25, 2025, when his previous term expired. Consideration of a Serious Crime Prevention Order was postponed until Nov. 17. The case demonstrates how cryptocurrency theft can extend beyond compromised software into physical coercion. Despite elaborate preparation and technical expertise, the operation ultimately failed because its intended victims maintained control of their front door.

title: Nomura explores sale of crypto unit Laser Digital: Bloomberg
summary: The potential sale of Laser Digital follows a fourth straight quarterly loss for Nomura’s European operations.
content:
Japanese financial services giant Nomura Holdings is reportedly weighing a sale of its cryptocurrency subsidiary Laser Digital as Nomura’s European operations continue to post losses.

Nomura has held talks with potential buyers, including Marex Group, Bloomberg reported Wednesday. The company has yet to make a final decision and could keep the business, according to the report.

Nomura’s European businesses posted a pretax loss of 7.4 billion yen ($46.5 million) in the quarter ended Sept. 30, 2026, their fourth consecutive quarterly loss. The company posted pretax profits in every other reporting region over the same period. Nomura did not disclose whether Laser Digital, which is headquartered in Switzerland, contributed to the European result.

Nomura is one of Japan’s largest financial services groups, with its investment management division overseeing 152.8 trillion yen ($960 billion) in assets as of September 2026.

The potential sale comes less than three months after Laser Digital Japan secured the country’s first new crypto exchange license in four years, allowing the firm to expand its institutional crypto trading services in Japan.

Established in 2022, Laser Digital provides institutional cryptocurrency trading, asset management and venture investment services. The company has also pursued expansion in the United States, receiving preliminary approval from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for its proposed national trust bank in May.

During a January earnings call, chief financial officer Hiroyuki Moriuchi said the company would reduce its cryptocurrency trading positions to limit short-term volatility while continuing to expand Laser Digital over the medium to long term.

title: US data center restrictions could give Bitcoin miners an edge in AI, though challenges remain
summary: As US voters push back against new data centers, Bitcoin miners already expanding into AI could benefit from their existing facilities.
content:
Bitcoin miners with power already secured could have an edge in the race to build AI data centers after voters in several US communities backed limits on new development. The midterms could also bring closer scrutiny from Congress over who pays for the grid upgrades those facilities need, industry experts told Cointelegraph.

Voters in several states weighed in on data center development during the Nov. 3 US midterms, when local measures appeared on the same ballots as congressional races. Amid concerns about rising electricity costs, water use and the impact on nearby communities, voters favored limiting development in 40 of the 41 local contests tracked by Ballotpedia.

The restrictions include citywide bans, limits on larger facilities, temporary pauses on new projects and voter approval requirements for some developments.

The results come as major Bitcoin mining companies continue moving into AI, a transition Jamie Brown, CEO of Global Kiwi Labs, said could become more attractive as local restrictions make it harder to build new data centers.

“If a Bitcoin miner has not yet repurposed their electric contract and physical plant to AI, the case to do so just got more compelling,” said Brown, whose company hosts servers for crypto exchanges and trading firms.

Related: US midterm elections 2026 as it happened: Democrats win control of Congress

Local restrictions make expansion harder

Miners’ shift to AI infrastructure is already underway, with publicly listed Bitcoin miners announcing more than $70 billion in AI and advanced computing contracts during 2025 and early 2026, according to a first-quarter report by CoinShares.

But state and local decisions can have a more immediate impact on whether data center projects move forward. That’s because local authorities often oversee zoning and building permits and can influence access to electricity.

“A company might have access to an attractive site and a significant amount of power capacity, but if local restrictions prevent it from expanding or upgrading that infrastructure, the opportunity becomes much more difficult to pursue,” said Jordan Knecht, head of strategic integrations at Kresus, a blockchain infrastructure company.

Last week, voters backed 27 measures to limit or oppose new data centers in the elections, according to Ballotpedia. These included five complete bans, 12 partial bans and six-month pauses on new projects in three Maine towns.

In Grove City, Ohio, voters approved a rule requiring public approval for large projects that use more than 20 megawatts of electricity, among other conditions.

“Federal policy will certainly influence the broader investment environment, but the practical ability to develop and operate these facilities often comes down to conditions in individual markets,” Knecht told Cointelegraph. “For miners looking to transition into AI, I think understanding those local dynamics will be just as important as following developments in Washington.”

Expanding into AI is not that simple

Building AI-ready data center infrastructure can cost between $8 million and $15 million per megawatt, compared with $700,000 to $1 million per megawatt for traditional mining facilities, according to a 2026 report by CoinShares.

That gap helps explain why a site with power already secured is only a starting point for miners moving into AI. “Transitioning from Bitcoin mining to AI workloads requires significant additional investment in infrastructure for cooling, networking, and reliability,” Knecht said.

Yuliya Barabash, founder of SBSB Fintech Lawyers, also pointed to differences in electricity needs between Bitcoin mining and AI data centers. Bitcoin miners can often reduce electricity use when prices rise, while AI data centers typically need a consistent power supply, she said.

“Higher electricity prices and additional regulatory requirements could make some projects less profitable or delay their implementation,” Barabash told Cointelegraph.

This comes as electricity demand from US data centers is also expected to rise, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA). The agency estimates that data centers used 224 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, a figure projected to nearly double to 426 terawatt-hours by 2030.

The impact of Congressional changes

One question facing the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress is who should pay to expand the grid for large data centers.

Knecht said lawmakers could take a closer look at how those projects affect electricity costs and how they get approved. “There may be more pressure to ensure that large data center operators are paying their fair share of infrastructure costs rather than passing those expenses on to consumers.”

Barabash also expects scrutiny of who pays for the electricity infrastructure needed to support data centers. “One of the key priorities is likely to be ensuring that technology companies, rather than ordinary consumers, bear the costs of the additional electricity infrastructure their facilities require,” she said.

Still, experts noted that closer attention does not necessarily mean Congress will discourage data center development. “AI infrastructure is becoming increasingly important to the US economy, and there is still a strong incentive to support investment in domestic computing capacity,” Knecht said.

For miners weighing a conversion, the question is whether AI revenue can justify the cost of upgrading cooling, networking and power systems. Brown thinks it can. “Miners will swap to AI because it is a better ROI than mining,” he said.

The post Binance Margin Trading Guide: How It Works and Key Tips for Crypto Traders in 2026 appeared first on CryptoNinjas.
content:
Binance margin trading is a trading strategy on Binance that allows traders to borrow crypto to trade with more capital than they currently own. Here, you use the crypto in your account as collateral and borrow extra funds to open larger trades with up to 20x leverage.

Using margin on Binance allows you to increase your trade size, take advantage of price movements, and manage positions without needing to sell your long-term holdings. 

It also gives you more room to hedge or adjust your trades quickly. This means you can earn more from a good setup, but you also carry the risk of losing borrowed funds. For instance, if your margin level drops too low, Binance can forcibly close your trade to recover the loan.

For a better understanding of Binance margin trading, this guide explains how Binance margin trading works, the fees and interest rates of margin trading on Binance, and how it compares to spot and futures trading. You will also learn how to set up your margin account, move funds, and place your first trade.

    • What Are the Borrowing Limits for Binance Margin Trading?
